BASIC TISSUES__Foundations of Histology:
What Histology Is & How a Slide Is Made

Histology is the study of tissues under the microscope — the bridge between naked-eye anatomy and cell biology. Almost every slide you meet is a thin, stained slice of tissue on glass, and knowing how it was made explains most of what you see (and most artefacts).

A biopsy becomes a slide through a fixed pipeline — each step preserves structure and makes cells visible.
1
Fixation10% neutral-buffered formalin: cross-links proteins, halts autolysis & decay, hardens tissue
↓
2
Dehydration & clearingGraded alcohols remove water; xylene clears the alcohol so wax can infiltrate
↓
3
EmbeddingTissue set in a paraffin wax block for support
↓
4
MicrotomyCut into 3–5 µm sections and floated onto a slide
↓
5
Rehydrate, stain, mountWax removed, tissue rehydrated, stained (usually H&E), sealed under a coverslip
Frozen section is the fast route — tissue is snap-frozen and cut on a cryostat, skipping wax. It gives a diagnosis in minutes (intra-operative margin assessment) and is the only way to preserve lipids and many enzymes, at the cost of poorer morphology.
H&E — The Workhorse Stain ⭐

Haematoxylin & Eosin stains >95% of routine slides. Two dyes of opposite charge partition the tissue by chemistry:

🔬 Image slot — a labelled H&E section showing blue nuclei & pink cytoplasm
🔵 Haematoxylin → basophilic (blue–purple)
  • A basic dye binding acidic (negatively charged) structures
  • Nuclei / chromatin & nucleoli (DNA)
  • Rough ER & ribosomes (RNA) → blue cytoplasm in secretory cells
  • Cartilage matrix, calcium, some mucins
🔴 Eosin → eosinophilic / acidophilic (pink)
  • An acidic dye binding basic (positively charged) proteins
  • Cytoplasm (most proteins), collagen, muscle
  • Red blood cells (brilliant pink), keratin
  • Most extracellular matrix
Read the colours as chemistry: "blue = nucleic-acid–rich", so a cell with blue cytoplasm is busy making protein (plasma cell, pancreatic acinar cell); "pink = protein-rich cytoplasm/matrix".
Special Stains — When H&E Isn't Enough

Ordered to show a specific substance, fibre or organism. Learn them as target → colour:

StainHighlightsResult & classic use
PAS (periodic acid–Schiff)Glycogen, basement membranes, mucins, fungiMagenta. Add diastase: magenta gone = it was glycogen (PAS-D). Thick GBM in diabetic nephropathy.
Masson's trichromeCollagen vs muscleCollagen blue/green, muscle & cytoplasm red. Grades fibrosis (cirrhosis).
Reticulin (silver)Reticular (type III) fibresBlack mesh — architecture of liver, marrow, lymph node.
Elastic (Verhoeff / EVG)Elastic fibresBlack. Elastic arteries, skin; loss in aneurysm.
Perls' Prussian blueFerric iron / haemosiderinBlue. Haemochromatosis, old haemorrhage.
Congo redAmyloidRed in bright field; apple-green birefringence under polarised light — diagnostic.
Ziehl–NeelsenAcid-fast bacilliRed rods on blue — TB & other mycobacteria.
Giemsa / WrightBlood & marrow films, parasites, H. pyloriDifferential staining of leucocytes & organisms.
Oil Red O / SudanLipidsRed — needs frozen tissue (wax dissolves fat).
Toluidine blueMast-cell granulesMetachromasia — granules purple, not blue.
🔬 Image slot — a special-stains comparison plate (PAS / trichrome / Congo red / ZN)
Three that win exam questions: Congo red → amyloid (apple-green birefringence) · Ziehl–Neelsen → TB · PAS → fungi & basement membrane.
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)

Uses labelled antibodies to detect specific antigens — it answers "what kind of cell is this?", above all when classifying a tumour of uncertain origin.

Cytokeratins (CK) → epithelial → carcinoma
Vimentin → mesenchymal (sarcoma)
CD45 (LCA) → leucocytes → lymphoma
S100 → melanoma, nerve, cartilage
Ki-67 → proliferation index (grade)
ER / PR / HER2 → breast cancer, guides therapy
IHC turns morphology into a lineage diagnosis and increasingly a treatment decision (HER2-positive breast cancer → trastuzumab).
How to Read a Slide — A Systematic Approach ⭐

Never start on high power. Zoom out to orient, then in to identify.

🔬 Image slot — same field at low vs high power to show the zoom-out-then-in approach
1
Low power — orientation & architectureIs there a capsule? Overall pattern — layered tube (GI), lobules (gland/liver), follicles (thyroid/lymph node), tubules (kidney/testis)? First guess at the organ.
↓
2
Medium power — functional unitFind the repeating unit: villus + crypt, glomerulus + tubules, seminiferous tubule, gastric gland. Identify the lining epithelium.
↓
3
High power — cells & specialisationsName the cell types; read the nuclei; spot cilia, brush border, striations, secretory granules, keratin.
The four questions that name most tissue
Epithelium or connective tissue? Cells packed with little matrix vs sparse cells in abundant matrix.
Simple or stratified? One layer (absorb/secrete) vs many (protect).
Cell shape? Squamous, cuboidal or columnar → names the epithelium.
Surface specialisation? Cilia (airway), brush border (gut/kidney), keratin (skin).
Microscopy & Resolution
🔬 Light microscope
  • Total magnification = objective × eyepiece (40× × 10× = 400×)
  • Useful to ~1000×; resolution ~0.2 µm (limited by the wavelength of light)
  • Shows cells, nuclei, tissue architecture
⚛️ Electron microscope
  • TEM → ultrastructure: organelles, basement membrane, cell junctions, cilia axoneme (9+2)
  • SEM → 3-D surface
  • Resolution to ~0.2 nm (electrons have a far shorter wavelength)
When you NEED EM: a filtration-barrier lesion on renal biopsy (podocyte foot processes, GBM), primary ciliary dyskinesia (absent dynein arms), and junctions/granules too small for light microscopy.
Artefacts — Don't Call Them Pathology
  • Folds & tears — from cutting/floating
  • Knife (chatter) marks — parallel lines from a nicked blade
  • Shrinkage clefts — white spaces around cells
  • Air bubbles under the coverslip
  • Formalin pigment — brown/black granules
  • Freezing artefact — ice-crystal holes
If a "lesion" is perfectly straight, perfectly round, or sits partly off the tissue, suspect an artefact — not disease.
Clinical Correlate — From Biopsy to Diagnosis

Histology is the diagnosis in much of medicine — a cancer is defined by what the pathologist sees.

Routine biopsy
Formalin → wax → H&E → report on cell type, grade, margins, invasion.
Frozen section
Minutes, intra-operative — "is this tumour?", "are the margins clear?"
Special stains
Congo red → amyloid; ZN → TB; PAS-D → fungi / storage; Perls' → iron.
IHC / molecular
Tumour lineage & therapy targets (ER/PR/HER2, Ki-67).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Basophilic = blue (nuclei, RER/ribosomes, DNA/RNA); eosinophilic = pink (cytoplasmic protein, collagen, muscle, RBC).
  • Routine fixative = 10% neutral-buffered formalin; sections cut at 3–5 µm.
  • Lipids need frozen sections (Oil Red O / Sudan) — wax dissolves fat.
  • Congo red + apple-green birefringence = amyloid.
  • PAS → glycogen, basement membrane, fungi; PAS-diastase removes glycogen to confirm it.
  • Masson's trichrome grades fibrosis (collagen blue/green).
  • Light microscopy resolution ~0.2 µm; use EM for basement membrane, cilia & junctions.
  • Always read low power first — architecture before cytology.

BASIC TISSUES__Bone (compact, cancellous:
Overview — Bone as a Mineralised Connective Tissue

Bone is a specialised connective tissue whose defining feature is a calcified extracellular matrix — this is what makes it rigid, unlike every other connective tissue.

🔬 Image slot — long-bone structure / bone composition overview
Functions
Support & protection — skeleton, skull, thoracic cage
Movement — levers & muscle attachment
Mineral reservoir — ~99% of body calcium & phosphate; central to Ca²⁺ homeostasis
Haematopoiesis — houses red marrow
Endocrine — osteocalcin (metabolism), FGF23 (phosphate)
Matrix composition
Organic (~35%) — osteoid
  • Type I collagen (~90% of organic)
  • Ground substance: proteoglycans + glycoproteins (osteocalcin, osteonectin, osteopontin)
  • → tensile strength & flexibility
Inorganic (~65%) — mineral
  • Hydroxyapatite — Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂ crystals
  • Deposited on/along collagen fibrils
  • → compressive strength & hardness; mineral store
Reinforced-concrete analogy: collagen = the steel rods (resist stretching/tension); hydroxyapatite = the concrete (resists compression). Lose the mineral → rubbery bone (osteomalacia); lose/weaken the collagen → brittle bone (osteogenesis imperfecta).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
  • Pink (eosinophilic) mineralised matrix in lamellae — parallel/concentric layers
  • Osteocytes sitting in lacunae (small dark spaces), linked by fine canaliculi
  • In compact bone: concentric lamellae around a central canal = an osteon (Haversian system) — the give-away
🔬 Image slot — compact bone osteon / Haversian system (ground section)
Ground section (undecalcified)
  • Cells are lost; lacunae & canaliculi fill with air/debris → appear black
  • Best for showing osteon architecture
Decalcified H&E
  • Mineral removed so tissue can be cut
  • Shows cells — osteocytes, surface osteoblasts, marrow
Bone must be decalcified (EDTA/acid) or ground thin before sectioning — the mineral is too hard for a microtome.
Compact vs Cancellous Bone
🔬 Image slot — compact (cortical) vs cancellous (trabecular) bone comparison
Compact (cortical)
  • Dense outer shell of the bone
  • Organised into osteons; central Haversian canal (longitudinal neurovascular channel)
  • Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely, connecting Haversian canals & periosteum
  • Interstitial lamellae (old osteon remnants) fill the gaps; circumferential lamellae at outer/inner surfaces
  • ~80% of skeletal mass; slow turnover
Cancellous (spongy / trabecular)
  • Network of trabeculae with marrow-filled spaces
  • No osteons — trabeculae are thin and nourished by diffusion from marrow
  • Trabeculae align along lines of stress (Wolff's law)
  • ~20% of mass but ~90% of surface area → metabolically active, high turnover (hit first in osteoporosis)
The Bone Cells
CellOriginRole & appearance
OsteoprogenitorMesenchymal stem cell (periosteum, endosteum)Divides & differentiates into osteoblasts
OsteoblastFrom osteoprogenitorBone-forming. Cuboidal, basophilic cytoplasm (abundant RER); secrete osteoid & initiate mineralisation; line bone surfaces
OsteocyteOsteoblast trapped in matrixMature cell in a lacuna; processes in canaliculi; maintain matrix & act as mechanosensors that direct remodelling
OsteoclastMonocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineageBone-resorbing. Large, multinucleated; sit in Howship's lacunae; ruffled border secretes H⁺ (dissolves mineral) + cathepsin K (digests collagen)
🔬 Image slot — osteoclast in a Howship's lacuna & osteoblasts lining osteoid
RANK–RANKL–OPG axis: osteoblasts express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast formation & activation. OPG is a decoy receptor that blocks this. PTH & vitamin D raise RANKL → more resorption. (Denosumab is an anti-RANKL drug.)
Periosteum & Endosteum
Periosteum
  • Covers the external surface (except articular cartilage)
  • Outer fibrous layer + inner osteogenic (cambium) layer of osteoprogenitors
  • Anchored by Sharpey's fibres; richly vascular & sensory (pain)
Endosteum
  • Thin lining of internal surfaces — medullary cavity, Haversian canals, trabeculae
  • Osteoprogenitor + bone-lining cells
Bone Formation (Ossification)
Woven bone (immature)
  • Laid down rapidly; random collagen, more cells, weaker
  • Fetal skeleton, fracture callus, Paget's
Lamellar bone (mature)
  • Organised, parallel/concentric collagen; stronger
  • Progressively replaces woven bone
Two routes of formation
Intramembranous
  • Mesenchyme → osteoblasts → bone directly (no cartilage model)
  • Flat bones: skull vault, most facial bones, clavicle, mandible
Endochondral
  • Hyaline cartilage model is replaced by bone
  • Long bones, vertebrae, base of skull, most of the skeleton
  • Primary centre (diaphysis) + secondary centres (epiphyses)
🔬 Image slot — endochondral ossification & the epiphyseal growth-plate zones
Epiphyseal (growth) plate — 5 zones
1
Resting / reserveQuiescent hyaline cartilage; anchors the plate to the epiphysis
2
ProliferationChondrocytes divide and stack into columns → lengthening
3
HypertrophyChondrocytes enlarge
4
CalcificationCartilage matrix calcifies; chondrocytes die
5
OssificationOsteoblasts lay bone on the calcified cartilage spicules
The growth plate drives longitudinal growth and fuses after puberty (sex-steroid driven). Width of bone grows by appositional growth from the periosteum.
Bone Remodelling & Its Control

Bone is renewed lifelong by coupled resorption + formation at the Basic Multicellular Unit (BMU): osteoclasts resorb → reversal → osteoblasts form new osteoid → mineralisation. About 10% of the skeleton is replaced per year.

Repair microdamage
Adapt to load (Wolff's law)
Ca²⁺ homeostasis
Hormonal & mechanical control
FactorEffect on bone
PTH↑ resorption indirectly (osteoblast RANKL) → ↑ serum Ca²⁺. Intermittent low dose is anabolic (teriparatide)
Calcitriol (vit D)↑ gut Ca²⁺/PO₄ absorption → enables mineralisation; deficiency → osteomalacia/rickets
Calcitonin↓ osteoclast activity → ↓ serum Ca²⁺ (minor role in humans)
OestrogenRestrains resorption; menopausal loss → osteoporosis
Mechanical load↑ formation; immobility/microgravity → bone loss
Stains & Ultrastructure
  • Decalcified H&E — routine; shows cells & marrow
  • Ground section (undecalcified) — osteon detail; lacunae/canaliculi black
  • von Kossa — mineralised matrix black → distinguishes mineralised bone from unmineralised osteoid
  • Goldner's trichrome — mineralised bone green, osteoid red → diagnoses osteomalacia (wide red osteoid seams)
  • Tetracycline labelling — fluorescent; marks the mineralisation front to measure bone-formation rate
🔬 Image slot — von Kossa / Goldner's trichrome showing mineralised bone vs osteoid (optional)
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Osteoporosis
↓ bone mass, normal mineralisation; resorption > formation (age, menopause) → fragility fractures
Osteomalacia / Rickets
Defective mineralisation → excess unmineralised osteoid; vitamin D deficiency; soft bones
Paget's disease
Disordered, excessive remodelling; mosaic pattern of cement lines; enlarged weak bone
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Type I collagen defect → brittle bones, blue sclerae
Osteopetrosis
Osteoclast failure → dense but brittle bone, marrow crowding
Hyperparathyroidism
↑ resorption → osteitis fibrosa cystica, brown tumours
Fracture healing recapitulates development: haematoma → soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus → hard (woven-bone) callus → remodelling to lamellar bone.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Osteon (Haversian system) = structural unit of compact bone; cancellous bone has no osteons.
  • Osteoblast = basophilic, bone-forming; osteoclast = multinucleated, haematopoietic, resorbs in Howship's lacunae (cathepsin K + acid).
  • Only the osteoclast comes from the haematopoietic (monocyte) line — the rest are mesenchymal.
  • Volkmann's canals connect Haversian canals (transverse vs longitudinal).
  • Intramembranous = flat bones; endochondral = long bones (cartilage model).
  • Growth plate zones: Resting → Proliferation → Hypertrophy → Calcification → Ossification.
  • Osteoporosis = ↓ mass (normal mineralisation); osteomalacia = defective mineralisation (excess osteoid).
  • von Kossa blackens mineral; Goldner's separates mineralised bone (green) from osteoid (red).
  • Bone must be decalcified or ground before sectioning.
